title: Dolores Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Dolores wells have a 104-foot median depth; see local yields, water levels, drilling costs, permit history, and risks before buying.
h1: Wells Around Dolores, Colorado: Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Well records within 5 miles of Dolores show a wide range of conditions. The median recorded depth is 104 feet, but some wells reach 1,225 feet. Reported yields are generally useful for household wells, although the available yield data covers only 37 wells.

Most permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, so nearby results are helpful but not a guarantee for a particular lot. Before buying or building, review neighboring well records, confirm the intended use with Colorado DWR, and budget for a complete water system rather than drilling alone.

sections.heading: How deep are wells around Dolores?
sections.html:
Dolores-area well depth is variable. The median recorded depth is 104 feet, and the middle half runs from 41 to 258 feet. That means a driller bidding a typical site may be working in a relatively shallow range, but the spread is large enough that a single flat depth assumption is risky.

The depth mix shows that 48% of recorded wells are under 100 feet, while 31% fall between 100 and 300 feet. Another 11% are between 300 and 600 feet, and 10% exceed 600 feet. The deepest record is 1,225 feet. Local geology, fractures, valley sediments, and the exact well location can all change the result.

sections.heading: What water yield can a Dolores well provide?
sections.html:
The reported yield median is 12.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 6.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. That is a useful range for many domestic systems, but yield is not the same as storage in the pressure tank or household water demand.

Of the wells reporting yield, 51% produced between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 38% reported more than 15 gallons per minute. Still, 8% were under 1 gallon per minute, with another 3% between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. Ask for the well test, pump setting, and recovery information. A low-yield well may work with storage, but it changes system design and operating expectations.

sections.heading: Water levels and groundwater trend near Dolores
sections.html:
Only 11 records report a static water level, so the water-level sample is limited. Among those records, the median depth to water is 9 feet, with the middle half from 7 to 24 feet. Those measurements suggest shallow static water in the reported wells, but they should not be treated as a guaranteed depth to water on an untested parcel.

The permit counts by decade do not show groundwater levels. They show 6 permits in the 1960s, 17 in the 1970s, 22 in the 1980s, 37 in the 1990s, 39 in the 2000s, 32 in the 2010s, and 17 in the 2020s. This dataset does not establish a dropping water table.

sections.heading: Who has drilled near Dolores, and when?
sections.html:
Colorado DWR records contain 236 permitted wells within the study area. Of those, 155 are recorded as constructed and 158 report a total depth. The newest permit year is 2025, so the area has continued to see well permitting rather than being represented only by older construction.

The most active drillers in these records are Mcpherson Drilling Co. (Mcpherson, Billy G.) with 37 wells, Ancell Drilling Service (Ancell, Lee) with 16, and Ucolo Drilling LLC (Redshaw, Richard R.) with 14. A permit history identifies who appears in the records; it is not a recommendation or a substitute for checking current licensing, availability, and references.

sections.heading: What does a new well cost near Dolores?
sections.html:
The local cost model uses a typical drilling rate of $50–$75 per foot for mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. At the 104-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $5,200–$7,800. That is the drilling portion, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at about $11,200–$19,800 at the median depth. A deeper hole, difficult access, casing and grout requirements, or added treatment can move the bid outside that range. Have the driller separate footage, casing, grout, development, pump equipment, trenching, electrical, and testing so competing bids cover the same work.

sections.heading: Risks to check before building around Dolores
sections.html:
Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer: 228 wells are in that category. Fractured rock can produce very different results between nearby lots, so a neighboring high-yield well does not guarantee the same outcome. There are also 11 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 3 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site mapped within about 10 miles. Check site-specific water testing and environmental records before closing.

Low-yield wells, dry holes, water quality, casing, grout, and septic separation all deserve review. A septic system and the house location need adequate usable ground, access, and drainage. Colorado DWR permits control the authorized use. Exempt household-use wells have a 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit, and an augmentation plan may be needed in an over-appropriated basin.

sections.heading: Buying or building a lot near Dolores
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, then compare nearby permitted wells rather than relying on the area median alone. Review construction depth, reported yield, static water level, aquifer description, permit status, and intended use. The records show 71% domestic or household use, 4% stock, 2% irrigation, and 17% monitoring, so a permit's purpose matters when comparing it with a home site.

For a purchase, make well inspection, water testing, permit review, and septic feasibility part of due diligence. For new construction, get a driller's site-specific opinion before finalizing the house, driveway, septic field, and utility trench layout. The same approach applies in Lewis, Cortez, and Mancos, but conditions can change quickly outside the Dolores study area.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Dolores, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth within 5 miles of Dolores is 104 feet. The middle half runs from 41 to 258 feet. About 48% are under 100 feet, while 10% exceed 600 feet. The deepest record is 1,225 feet, so a nearby well is useful evidence but cannot set the exact depth for a new lot.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Dolores?
faq.a: The local model uses $50–$75 per foot. At the 104-foot median depth, drilling alone is estimated at $5,200–$7,800. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $11,200–$19,800. Deeper drilling, access problems, casing, grout, and site-specific construction can change the final bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Dolores?
faq.a: The reported yield median is 12.0 gallons per minute, with a middle-half range of 6.0–15.0 gallons per minute. About 8% of reported-yield wells produce under 1 gallon per minute, while 38% exceed 15 gallons per minute. Only 37 wells report yield, so request a test for the specific property.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Dolores, Colorado?
faq.a: The records identify 11 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 3 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site within about 10 miles. That does not determine a particular home's water quality. Test the well for relevant contaminants, review environmental records, and confirm the well's construction and septic conditions before relying on the water.

faq.q: Are water levels dropping near Dolores?
faq.a: The available records do not establish a declining water table. Only 11 wells report static water level; their median depth to water is 9 feet, with a middle-half range of 7–24 feet. Permit counts by decade describe drilling activity, not groundwater change. A local hydrogeologist or well professional can evaluate site-specific measurements.
